recent.question: Will Alexia Putellas win the 2026 Women's Ballon d'Or?
recent.what_happened: We were given that the outcome was YES: Putellas won the 2026 Women's Ballon d'Or at the London ceremony on 26 October. I could not confirm this myself, because my search only turned up coverage from before the ceremony. Her case was strong: she won five trophies with Barcelona, had a competition-high 14 goal contributions in the Champions League, was named its Player of the Season, and the three-time winner Bonmatí was off the shortlist.
recent.what_we_missed: The market had Putellas at about 93% and the forecaster said 42%. The forecaster seems to have treated Pajor, Pina and the other Barcelona players as serious rivals, when the facts it had already pointed to one clear favourite: the UWCL Player of the Season on a treble-plus team, with the dominant winner gone. It also appears not to have checked bookmaker odds, power rankings or reported leaks, which almost certainly showed her as the overwhelming favourite.
recent.lesson: For voted awards where one candidate holds the main season honours and the usual winner is absent, check bookmaker odds and media power rankings before forecasting. Treat a market price above 90% as strong evidence unless you have a concrete reason to bet against it.

suggested_change.change: For award-voting questions, always pull current bookmaker odds and major outlets' power rankings. If the forecast is more than 30 points away from the market, write down the specific reason why.

recent.question: Will Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva win the second round of the 2026 Brazilian presidential election by less than 4%?
recent.what_happened: Lula won the October 25 runoff by about 2 points of the valid vote (live TSE counts with 60–73% of sections in showed roughly 50.5–51.0% to 49.0–49.5%), even though every poll released after the first round had Flávio ahead by 4–5.6 points. Flávio had also beaten the polls in the first round. I only found partial counts, not the final certified total.
recent.what_we_missed: Most of Lula's winning outcomes fell in this bracket, so the question was really whether Lula would win at all. Two things may have deserved more weight: a 4–5 point poll lead with 2+ weeks to go is not decisive in Brazil, and Brazil's polarized runoffs tend to tighten. Even so, the post-first-round evidence pointed clearly toward Flávio. At 23% the forecast was already more than double the market's 10.5%, and that was the better side.
recent.lesson: In a polarized runoff where the leader is ahead by only 4–6 points two weeks out, assume a wide spread of outcomes (a standard deviation of about 4–5 points on the margin). Don't push the trailing candidate's narrow-win bracket much below 20–25% just because polls missed in one direction in the first round.

suggested_change.change: None needed. The forecast was reasonably calibrated and beat the market, and the less likely outcome happened.

recent.question: Bitcoin price on Oct 16, 2026? ($83,000 or above)
recent.what_happened: BTC traded around $82,500–83,100 from Oct 9–11, almost exactly at the real $83,000 strike, and the 60-second BRTI average at 5 PM EDT on Oct 16 came in below $83,000, so the market resolved NO. I could not find the exact Oct 16 price. A BGeometrics report puts BTC at about $83,031 on Oct 10, and an undated Changelly page shows about $84,692. The NO outcome is the only firm data point.
recent.what_we_missed: The research brief stated the strike wrongly as $80,000 in two places, the status summary and the rules note, while the question's strike is $83,000. That error made it look as if BTC was 3–4% in the money when it was really at the money. The final 0.5 suggests the forecaster used the right strike anyway, and it was closer to the outcome than the market's 0.58. The flawed brief was still a real risk.
recent.lesson: Before using any distance-to-strike figure, check the strike in the research notes against the question title and resolution threshold. In this ladder market, $83,000 means above $82,999.99, not $80,000.

suggested_change.change: Add an automated check that pulls the threshold out of the resolution rules and flags any research fact that names a different strike before the facts go to the forecaster.

recent.question: Will Elon Musk post 340-359 tweets from October 9 to October 16, 2026?
recent.what_happened: Musk's count for Oct 9–16, 2026 landed in the 340–359 bracket, so the market resolved YES. His pace stayed near the roughly 46–50 posts a day of the Oct 2–9 week (about 324 posts), not the 28–31 a day of late September. At judgment the market priced YES at only 6.45%; the researched forecast said 40% and the no-research forecast said 14%.
recent.what_we_missed: The forecast was right to be well above the market, but it still leaned the wrong way. It never got the live XTracker count for the first roughly 28 hours of the window (judged Oct 10 15:50Z), which would have shown whether he was on a ~340+ pace. It also weighed the old Sept 29–Oct 6 rate (200–219, from an unverified auto-generated page) against the newer and more relevant Oct 2–9 rate of about 324. The no-research forecast of 14% was anchored on the stale lower rate. The only outside snapshot I found was a third-party (PredScope) page from Oct 6, before the window opened, which favored 180–2
recent.lesson: For Musk tweet-count brackets judged partway through the window, pull the live in-window XTracker count and project it forward, putting most of the weight on the most recent 7 days rather than older weekly results.

suggested_change.change: For any Musk post-count market judged after the window opens, require fetching the current xtracker.polymarket.com count and elapsed time, and compute a projected total with a variance band before forecasting.

recent.question: Will Elon Musk post 280-299 tweets from October 9 to October 16, 2026?
recent.what_happened: Musk's posting sped up during the window and the market settled on the 340–359 bracket at about 100% around the Oct 16 close. The final count was above 340, so the 280–299 bracket we forecast resolved NO.
recent.what_we_missed: Putting 51% on a single 20-post bracket with six days left was too confident. The base rates we had conflicted: one source put the prior week at 200–219 and another at about 324. The market priced this bracket at only 7.5%, which most likely reflected the live XTracker count for the first day and an expected pace above 300. We never checked that count.
recent.lesson: With most of a weekly window still to run, keep any single 20-post bracket at roughly 30% or less, and treat a large gap from the market price (here 51% vs 7.5%) as a signal to check the live tracker count before departing from the market.

suggested_change.change: Cap single-bracket probabilities on Musk tweet-count markets when more than three days remain, and require a check of the live XTracker count whenever the forecast differs from the market by more than 3x.

recent.question: Will Douglas Ruas win the Governor of Rio de Janeiro election?
recent.what_happened: Ruas led the October 4 first round with 49.27% to Paes's 42.76%, even though every final poll had Paes ahead by about 8 points. The electoral court then annulled Garotinho's roughly 3% of the vote, which lifted Ruas to 50.88% of valid votes. TRE-RJ proclaimed him elected in the first round and Paes conceded.
recent.what_we_missed: The forecaster relied on an unverified search snippet claiming Paes had won outright with more than 60%, which was false, and set 8% against the market's 16.7%. It also underweighted two things: Brazilian polls can miss right-wing candidates by a lot, and annulling Garotinho's votes shrinks the valid-vote base for whoever is leading, not only for Paes.
recent.lesson: Never let an unverifiable snippet about a result move a forecast made while voting is still open, and on election day don't go well below the market without verified results.

suggested_change.change: Mark any unverified claim about results that predates the official count as inadmissible, and before judging on election day, check TSE or TRE live results or wait until polls close.

recent_wins.question: Will Eduardo Paes win the Governor of Rio de Janeiro election?
recent_wins.what_happened: In the October 4 first round, Douglas Ruas (PL) finished first with about 49.3% of valid votes and Eduardo Paes about 42.8%, so the race goes to a runoff on October 25. That result reverses the final polls, which had Paes ahead by 8–10 points. 274,411 votes for Garotinho are still sub judice, and some outlets reported that how the TSE counts them could even decide the race for Ruas outright. The resolution recorded here is 'no', although as of Oct 16 the runoff had not yet been held.
recent_wins.what_worked: The forecaster treated the October 5 question close as meaning Paes had to win outright in the first round. With polls putting him at roughly 46–52% of valid votes, that made a YES much less certain than the market's 82% implied. It also correctly ignored the unverified Substack claim that Paes won with over 60%. But the actual miss came from a polling error of roughly 15 points on the margin, which no fact in the research foresaw. So the 0.19 landed for reasons the forecaster didn't anticipate.
recent_wins.lesson: When a question's close date falls before the runoff, work out the probability of an outright first-round win separately from the probability of winning the race overall, and price in Brazilian polls' history of underrating PL/Bolsonaro-aligned candidates.

suggested_change.change: Flag questions where the resolution text ('winner of this election', runoff included) clashes with an early close date. Make the forecaster state which reading it is using, and check that the recorded outcome isn't premature before the runoff on October 25.

recent_wins.question: Cleveland wins
recent_wins.what_happened: Cleveland beat the White Sox 2-0 in ALDS Game 5 at Progressive Field on Oct 10, 2026, coming back from 0-2 down in the series. Gavin Williams struck out 12, tying the franchise record, and José Ramírez hit a two-run homer in the 4th, the only runs of the game.
recent_wins.what_worked: With research the forecaster said 64%, against 56.5% for the market and 34% without research. It correctly picked out home field, Cleveland's momentum after Games 3 and 4, Williams as the likely starter with his AL-leading strikeout numbers and 11 strikeouts in Game 2, and a tired White Sox bullpen. Still, a single winner-take-all baseball game at 64% is close to a coin flip, and a 2-0 game could easily have gone the other way.
recent_wins.lesson: In single-elimination baseball games, treat a starter edge plus home field as a small move of a few points over the market, and size bets to match rather than calling it strong evidence.

suggested_change.change: Limit bet size when our probability is within about 10 points of a market priced between 40% and 60% on a single MLB game, since the result is mostly variance.

recent_wins.question: Marshall wins by over 4.5 points
recent_wins.what_happened: The question resolved NO: Marshall did not win the October 10, 2026 home game against Coastal Carolina by more than 4.5 points. I could not find the final score, so I can't say whether Marshall won narrowly, pushed toward the line, or lost.
recent_wins.what_worked: With research, the forecast came down to 0.28 from about 0.40. Several facts pushed it lower: Marshall had won its three games by 2, 6 and 1 points; it allowed 35 points a game while Coastal Carolina allowed 25; Coastal's three recent losses were all close; and Coastal had won 3 of the last 4 meetings. Still, the market's 0.495 put the line at roughly a fair spread, and covering a 4.5-point spread in college football is close to a coin flip, so most of the edge here was luck rather than proven skill.
recent_wins.lesson: When a spread market is priced near 50%, close margins in a team's wins plus a defense that gives up a lot of points are reasonable reasons to lean against the favorite covering. Size those bets modestly, because one game's margin is very noisy.

suggested_change.change: Cap the stake on spread-cover bets where the market is between 0.45 and 0.55 and the edge comes only from season-margin stats, unless the research turned up something like an injury or a quarterback change that the line hasn't priced in.

recent_wins.question: Will Atlanta United FC win on 2026-10-10?
recent_wins.what_happened: FC Cincinnati won 3-1 at Mercedes-Benz Stadium on Oct 10, 2026, with two goals from Kévin Denkey and a late one from Tom Barlow; Miguel Almirón scored Atlanta's only goal. Cincinnati won even without Evander, and the market resolved No.
recent_wins.what_worked: The researched forecast of 0.27, against a market price of 0.425 and 0.39 without research, rested on base rates. Atlanta had only 3 wins in their last 10 home games and sat 28th in the league. Cincinnati had lost just 1 of the last 9 meetings and had a decent record at Mercedes-Benz Stadium. The forecast also accounted for the fact that a draw counts as No. Cincinnati's five-game winless run and Evander's absence didn't outweigh those factors. Still, this is one match: even at the market's price, No was about 58% likely, so a fair share of this result was variance.
recent_wins.lesson: When a home team's own home record is poor and the head-to-head trend is lopsided, don't let it get credit for home advantage just for playing at home. Remember that the draw also pays No when the market prices a weak favorite above 40%.

suggested_change.change: Pull the home team's recent home-only record and the last 8–10 head-to-head results as standard inputs for single-match soccer win markets. Weigh them against the market's implied home advantage before reacting to injury news.

recent_wins.question: Will Manchester United FC win on 2026-10-10?
recent_wins.what_happened: The match at Old Trafford finished Manchester United 1–1 Tottenham. Mbeumo put United ahead in the 73rd minute, Bentancur was sent off, and Solanke headed in a 90+2 equaliser for 10-man Spurs, so the market resolved No.
recent_wins.what_worked: We put United at 0.43 against a market price of 0.565. That rested on real points: United had one win in five league games, a long injury list (Sesko, Dorgu, De Ligt, Ugarte, with Rashford, Mainoo and Amad doubtful), a poor recent record against Spurs, and a draw-prone Spurs side that kept clean sheets in two 0–0 games. Still, United led until stoppage time, so this No came from one late header and was close to a coin flip.
recent_wins.lesson: When a struggling favourite at home is priced above 55% to win, remember a draw also resolves No, and price it in explicitly (roughly 25–30% here) rather than letting the opponent's place in the table anchor the estimate.

suggested_change.change: Have the researcher give an explicit three-way estimate (win, draw, loss) from bookmaker odds or recent draw rates, so the gap with the market comes from stated numbers rather than a gut discount.

recent_wins.question: Will AFC Bournemouth win on 2026-10-10?
recent_wins.what_happened: Chelsea beat Bournemouth 5-1 at Stamford Bridge on 10 October 2026, so the question resolved No. Chelsea led 2-0 inside three minutes through Henderson and Rogers, João Pedro scored twice and Henderson added a late goal. Bournemouth are still without a Premier League win under Marco Rose after six matchdays.
recent_wins.what_worked: Research pulled the forecast down from 0.38 to 0.11, well below the market's 0.205. It found Bournemouth with no wins and a long list of injuries (Scott, Kluivert, Brooks, Kroupi and possibly Gittens), Chelsea's key players (Caicedo, Palmer, James, João Pedro) declared fit, and Chelsea unbeaten in 9 meetings. To be fair, the market also made No about an 80% favourite, so the edge over the market was modest. The lopsided score backs the research, but on its own it doesn't prove 0.11 was the better number.
recent_wins.lesson: When an away underdog is winless and missing several first-choice attackers while the home side gets its stars back, size the forecast mainly from the team news, not from the home side's recent form or leaky defence.

suggested_change.change: Always compare the two sides' injury and availability lists from the latest press conferences before forecasting a match, because here they mattered more than the head-to-head history or recent results.

rules.rule: Read crypto rules for the exact strike, venue/pair and test (any touch or a close at a set candle); if mid-window, first check the venue's candles or dated reports for whether the strike was already hit and by how much, then record a venue spot timestamped under an hour old.

For crypto threshold questions, report percent distance to strike, hours left, how many of the last 14 days the venue traded through that level, realized volatility, any weekend, and timestamped same-day catalysts (yields, dollar, ETF flows, jobs data) or state none found.

For match questions, report both sides' dated absences and returns from the latest press conferences, the stand-in and the absent player's actual recent output, settled from confirmed lineups; label all-time series and head-to-heads under about 10 games as weak.

For team win or spread questions, report the home side's home-only and the visitor's road-only records, goals or points allowed over the last 5, the last 8–10 meetings, schedule strength behind any record or margin (e.g. FCS foes, first FBS year), and whether a draw resolves No.

If any match or tournament stage started before the judgment time, get its live or final score and the bracket path so far from a tracker timestamped within the past hour (e.g. Liquipedia, BLAST.tv, league site); discard result snippets that are undated or dated before the start.

For game-total questions (goals or points), report both teams' recent game totals with dates, label a 3–4 game streak as a small sample, note weakened opponents in any blowout, and report each side's starting QB or key starter changes and defensive ranking.

For tennis completion questions, read which endings count, report the tour level's normal-finish share and each player's recent full matches, weigh only past-week injury or withdrawal news, and after start time check Tennis Explorer or ITF for w/o or ret. first.

For NFL player props, research the named player, never team D/ST rates: for TDs, his TDs per game this and last season, red-zone carries or targets and target share; for yardage, attempts per game and games past the line; plus the opponent's rank and injured defenders.

For single MMA fights, report each fighter's age, recent opponents and how those fights ended, and dated weigh-in or weight-cut news; label win streaks and common-opponent comparisons as weak evidence.

For single MLB games, report confirmed starters' ERA, ERA+ and recent starts, each bullpen's unavailable arms (injury, leave, short rest), season and road records, and form since Sept 1; label old-roster franchise streaks and series-level rates as not single-game evidence.

For playoff series, first get the live or final score of any game started before the judgment time, then report the series score, wins the trailer needs and where, the cited comeback rate for that deficit, game margins and season records; past seasons' playoffs are background.

For video view questions, check the channel's uploads since the question opened and report any new video's upload time, hours elapsed, views and climb rate first; build references only from first-168-hour counts of recent comparable uploads, not lifetime or undated totals.

For live-streamed challenge questions near the deadline, get the current attempt's status from the past 12 hours (stream VODs, streamers' socials, fan trackers): milestones reached, gear, deaths or resets, plus the participants' own past completions and times.

For Rotten Tomatoes score questions, read the year-specific film page named in the rules, record the score, review count and dated earlier readings showing drift, and count how many negative reviews would move it past the strike before the check time.

For reality-show elimination questions, confirm every fact names the asked contestant and their own pro partner, and report couples left, eliminations per episode, live shows in the window, and every couple's judges' scores and bottom-three history.

For earnings-beat questions, copy the EPS basis (GAAP diluted or adjusted) and strike from the rules, report the dated consensus and recent revisions, the last 4–8 quarters' actual-versus-consensus surprise percentages, and management's dated guidance or segment commentary.

For CPI questions, get the dated consensus and Cleveland Fed nowcast, rebuild the 12-month rate from NSA index levels incl. the month dropping out, find the monthly change the strike needs, and estimate it bottom-up: gas weight × AAA/EIA change plus typical core and food.

For elections, once voting starts take results only from the official count (e.g. TSE/TRE live page) and discard unverified snippets; report undecideds, endorsements, late dropouts, annulled or sub judice votes and the valid-vote base, and dated past poll-vs-result gaps.
